strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether learned spectral features of the partial covariance operator can yield scalable CI tests, connecting the classical kernel/HSIC line of work (Fukumizu, Zhang, Strobl, Huang) with modern contrastive representation learning (Kostic et al., 2024).

The bi-level formulation in Section 3 / Appendix A is a technically non-trivial and reasonably clean extension: the composition term Σ_XZ Σ_ZŸ does not admit an unbiased estimator, and the low-rank auxiliary problem with features w_θ(Z) of dimension 2d is a sensible way to handle it, with a complete derivation of the empirical losses.

The theoretical analysis (Lemmas B.2–B.5, Theorems 4.1–4.2) is largely self-contained, uses appropriate tools (Lindeberg–Feller CLT, covariance-operator concentration à la Koltchinskii–Lounici, perturbation bounds), and correctly identifies the regimes (d = o(√n), d² log n ≲ n) under which the off-diagonal terms of the projection matrix Q are negligible.

Framing validity and power through the representation error E_m is an honest way to side-step the Shah–Peters no-free-lunch obstruction without imposing Lipschitz-type structural conditions on P_{X|Z}, and the paper is appropriately calibrated in the abstract and contributions ('preliminary experiments', 'suggest').
weaknesses: The central guarantees are conditional on assumptions that are never verified for the proposed method. Theorem 4.1 requires E_m → 0 (consistency of the bi-level representation learning) and Assumption 4.1 requires the learned features u_θ(X), v_θ(Ÿ), w_θ(Z) to be K-sub-Gaussian. No result connects the empirical bi-level loss minimization (Algorithm 1) to a small E_m, and sub-Gaussianity of data-driven neural features is unverifiable in practice. If representation learning fails or produces heavy-tailed features, the chi-squared null calibration can break down. The 'rigorous statistical guarantees' are thus contingent on properties of a black-box training procedure whose behavior is never analyzed.

The empirical evaluation is far too thin to support the paper's central claims of scalability and practicality. There is a single synthetic benchmark (post-nonlinear model, N=1500), two figures, and the power figure (Fig. 3) shows all displayed methods at power ≈ 1.0 across all dimensions — i.e., the benchmark cannot discriminate between methods. Only 3 of the 8 claimed baselines appear to be shown. Despite 'Scalable' in the title and claims of GPU acceleration and scalability over kernel methods, no runtime/memory comparison is reported. The motivating cancer-genomics application (Barretina et al.) is never tested; there are no real-data experiments.

No hyperparameter sensitivity, ablations, or error bars: the choice of d (which enters the chi-squared quantile with d² degrees of freedom, while validity requires d = o(√n)), the regularization γ, network architectures, n_steps/n_steps_inner, and the train/test split ratio are all unreported. Without code or implementation details, reproducibility is poor for an empirical 'practical path' claim.

The power theorem (Thm 4.2) requires ε_n² ≥ dE_m² + (d² + log(δ⁻¹))/n with unspecified constants and proofs in Appendix B.9 that rely on informal steps (e.g., 'for some large enough numerical constant', normal approximation of the χ²_{d²} quantile). The finite-sample content of the result is therefore limited, and the bound in Lemma B.2 with a 1/ε Markov rate is quite crude relative to the claimed chi-squared limit.

Presentation has noticeable sloppiness for a theory-driven paper: dimension of w_θ stated as R^{2d} in the main text but R^d in Appendix A; repeated typos ('have have', 'union bound over gives', 'Tbn is computing', 'hypotheis', inconsistent c_α vs c_α); Lemma B.3 statement mixes assumptions in a confusing way (contiguity is introduced in B.1 but never actually used); Eq. (24) eigenvalue indexing is awkward.

Related-work positioning overstates novelty in places: the operator characterization of CI via partial covariance is standard (Fukumizu et al. 2007; Strobl et al. 2019; Huang et al. 2022), and the spectral contrastive loss machinery is directly imported from Kostic et al. (2024); the genuinely new elements are the bi-level extension for the partial operator and the test-theoretic analysis, which is a solid but incremental contribution.

The stated contribution that 'restrictive structural assumptions hinder adaptation' is asserted rather than demonstrated: no experiment shows a setting where regression-based (GCM/KCIT) or permutation-based tests provably fail but SpecCIT succeeds; Fig. 2 actually shows KCIT failing type I control while GCIT succeeds, which complicates the narrative without being analyzed.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and well-motivated: recasting conditional independence testing through the partial covariance operator and using learned spectral features to address the known scalability and adaptivity limits of kernel CI tests is a promising direction.

The derivation of the bi-level contrastive formulation for learning the leading singular functions of Σ_{XY·Z} (Section 3, Appendix A) is technically nontrivial, extending the spectral representation learning framework of Kostic et al. (2024) to the partial covariance setting, which introduces genuine complications (the bias term involving Σ_XZ Σ_ZY).

The paper provides asymptotic theory for the proposed statistic: convergence to a chi-squared distribution with d² degrees of freedom under the null (Theorem 4.1) and a non-asymptotic power guarantee (Theorem 4.2), with proofs carried out in reasonable detail in the appendix.

The authors are candid that the experiments are 'preliminary,' and the framing of validity/power in terms of the representation quality rate ε_m rather than restrictive structural assumptions on P_{X,Y,Z} is a sensible and honest analysis strategy in light of the Shah & Peters (2020) hardness result.
weaknesses: The central claims are not fully supported by the evidence. The paper's headline claim — scalability — is never tested: there are no runtime/wall-clock comparisons against baselines and no experiments demonstrating scaling to large samples or high-dimensional conditioning sets. The empirical evaluation consists of a single synthetic post-nonlinear benchmark with N=1500, which is too limited to substantiate the abstract's claims of a 'practical and statistically grounded path toward scalable CI testing.'

The type I error guarantee is essentially conditional: Theorem 4.1 requires ε_m → 0, i.e., that the proposed bi-level representation learning algorithm is consistent. No result establishes that Algorithm 1 actually achieves ε_m → 0 (the bi-level optimization with non-convex neural networks is only heuristically justified). Similarly, Assumption 4.1 (sub-Gaussianity of learned neural features) is unverifiable and its interplay with the whitening post-processing step is not discussed. Thus the statistical validity of the deployed test rests on unproven algorithmic behavior.

The theoretical regime is restrictive relative to the 'scalable' framing: validity requires d = o(√n) and d² log(n)/n → 0 (Lemmas B.3, B.5), while the null distribution has d² degrees of freedom, so the calibration is reliable only in regimes where the test dimension is small relative to n. This limits practical applicability and is not confronted in the experiments.

The experiments lack the baselines the paper itself identifies as state of the art. Section 6 lists NNLSCIT, CD C, CCT, SCCIT, DG CIT, etc., but Figures 2–3 only compare against KCIT and GCIT. The power curves are saturated at ~1.0 for all methods across all settings, providing essentially no discriminative information about relative performance. There are no real-data experiments, despite the introduction motivating the method with a cancer cell-line drug response example.

Key algorithmic and experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing: network architectures, choice of output dimension d, regularization strength γ, number of inner/outer optimization steps, and how hyperparameters were selected are not reported. No code release is mentioned.

The bi-level formulation introduces an inner optimization (Eq. 6/14) whose solution the outer loss depends on; the paper does not analyze the effect of approximate inner solutions on the learned representations, nor does it empirically verify that the learned features recover the leading spectral subspaces (which the theory presumes).

The comparison to existing approaches is somewhat underdeveloped: the relationship between the proposed statistic and KCIT/RCIT-style random-feature tests, and precisely what is gained by learning rather than random features, is asserted (adaptivity to smoothness/sparsity/low-rank structure) but neither theoretically characterized nor demonstrated empirically.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: recasting CI testing through the partial covariance operator and using learned spectral features (building on Kostic et al., 2024) to gain adaptivity over fixed kernel bases is a natural but non-obvious bridge between kernel-based CI testing and modern representation learning.

The bi-level variational formulation (Eqs. 5-7) for learning the leading spectral features of the partial covariance operator is a genuine technical extension of the unconditional case, where the extra term involving Sigma_XZ Sigma_ZY breaks the standard spectral contrastive loss; the derivation in Appendix A is careful.

The theoretical analysis is substantive: the proof of the chi-squared null distribution (Thm 4.1) handles data-dependent learned features via concentration of the projection matrix Q (Lemma B.4), control of off-diagonal terms under the null, and a Lindeberg-Feller CLT (Lemma B.5). The power result (Thm 4.2) cleanly separates signal strength, representation error (d*eps_m), and estimation error (d^2/n), giving useful guidance on the choice of d.
The paper is honest that experiments are 'preliminary', positions the work against the Shah & Peters hardness result appropriately, and the related work section is thorough and well-organized.
weaknesses: The central claims of 'scalable and valid' are only partially supported. Validity is asymptotic and conditional on two unverifiable quantities: (i) the optimization gap eps_m -> 0 for the learned features (Eq. 9), which involves the true population operators and cannot be checked in practice, and (ii) Assumption 4.1 that the learned neural network features u_theta(X), v_theta(Y~), w_theta(Z) are K-sub-Gaussian, which is a strong assumption on trained networks that is neither verified empirically nor plausibly guaranteed by the training procedure. There is no convergence analysis of the bi-level Algorithm 1 itself, so the pipeline's end-to-end guarantee is assumption-stacked.

The experimental evidence is too thin for a main-track paper. Only one synthetic benchmark (post-nonlinear model) is used; the figures compare against only KCIT and GCIT despite listing many baselines (RCIT, RCCIT, KPCT, GCM, DGCIT, CDCT, NNLSCIT, CCIT); the power plot (Fig. 3) is saturated at ~1.0 for all methods and thus uninformative; the anomalous GCIT Type I error of ~0.9 at dim_z=10 in Fig. 2 is not explained. The motivating application (cancer cell line drug response) is never tested, and despite 'scalable' in the title, there are no runtime/wall-clock comparisons against kernel or permutation-based methods.

Finite-sample behavior of the chi-squared calibration is a concern: the theory requires d = o(sqrt(n)) and d^2 log(n)/n -> 0, but the choice of d (network output dimension) and other hyperparameters (architecture, gamma, split ratio m/n) are not reported. Unlike KCIT, no finite-sample correction (e.g., gamma approximation) is provided or evaluated, and Type I error is only assessed at one sample size.

The empirical whitenening post-processing and batch-level orthonormality regularization are justified only informally; it is asserted that whitening 'doesn't change the learned subspaces' and leaves the asymptotic theory intact, but this interaction (whitening with estimated covariance matrices on the training set, then computing the statistic on the test set) deserves explicit treatment in the theory.

Presentation issues: several typos ('We have have', 'that that'), Lemma B.3/B.5 duplicate definitions, Figure 3 conveys no information, and the abstract/introduction overstate maturity ('comprehensive theoretical analysis', 'practical and statistically grounded path') relative to what is delivered. No code or reproducibility statement is mentioned.

Significance is real but currently modest: the contribution is an interesting framework plus conditional guarantees, rather than a validated practical test; as it stands, practitioners cannot reliably build on it without knowing whether the assumptions hold in their setting.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem (scalable, valid conditional independence testing) and offers a principled bridge between classical partial-covariance-operator kernel tests (Fukumizu, Strobl et al.) and modern spectral/contrastive representation learning (Kostic et al. 2024, HaoChen et al. 2021). The bi-level variational formulation for learning the truncated SVD of the partial covariance operator is a genuine technical contribution over prior spectral feature learning for unconditional operators.

The theory is honest about the no-free-lunch results (Shah & Peters 2020) and instead frames validity and power via explicit representation-quality errors (E_val, E_pow) rather than imposing restrictive smoothness conditions on P_{X,Y|Z}. The chi-squared asymptotic null distribution (Theorem 4.1) and power characterization (Theorem 4.2) are reasonable and connect testing error to ML-aligned quantities.

Experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for a CI testing paper: multiple established baselines (KCIT, RCIT, GCIT, DGCIT, NNLSCIT, GCM, LPCIT), a shared tuning protocol with published hyperparameter grids, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (d, learning rate, regularization), a signal-strength ablation, a new nonsmooth high-dimensional benchmark, a Sachs-inspired CI-oracle experiment, runtime comparisons, and a real TCGA breast cancer application. The limitations section candidly acknowledges the lack of standard benchmarks and conservative calibration.

Reproducibility support is decent: implementation details, hyperparameter tables, computational environment, and a code repository are provided. The limitations discussion is honest (e.g., acknowledging that their assumptions for validity still exist and that calibration is conservative in practice).
weaknesses: The headline guarantees are weaker than the abstract suggests. Validity (Theorem 4.1) requires E_val -> 0, d = o(sqrt(n)), sqrt(d) E_m -> 0, and d^2 = o(n/log n), where E_m is an optimization/estimation error of the learned representations that is never bounded or even qualitatively controlled. The paper explicitly defers non-asymptotic rates for learned spectral representations to future work, so the theory ultimately conditions on uncontrolled learning success, and all guarantees are asymptotic with no finite-sample or bootstrap calibration.

Several proof steps are heuristic rather than rigorous. In the proof of Theorem 4.2, the chi-squared quantile is handled via a large-d normal approximation ('c_alpha ~= d^2 + 2d z_{1-alpha}') and the final power condition appears only at the level of order notation, with loose constant tracking. There are also typographical/notation errors that suggest insufficient polish (e.g., 'x ⊥⊥ ẏ| z' in Lemma B.3, repeated sentence in B.8, 'we have have' on p.17, the Lemma B.5 assumption stated as 'n >= c K^4 d^2 log n as n -> infinity').

The practical type I error control relies on asymptotic chi-squared calibration with learned, whitened features; the authors themselves concede conservative calibration in practice (also visible in Fig. 10), and there is no data-driven calibration alternative (e.g., permutation or bootstrap). This weakens the 'valid' part of the contribution relative to the title's claim.

Empirical results have gaps: (i) SpectralCIT loses power to KCIT at high conditioning dimensions (Fig. 5), and KCIT's failure is attributed to type I error; (ii) baseline tuning is uneven (DGCIT exposes few hyperparameters and is essentially untuned, LPCIT excluded for runtime); (iii) the TCGA breast cancer experiment is a single dataset with N=1341 triplets, a rejection by SpectralCIT but not by KCIT/NNLSCIT is a strong claim resting on asymptotic calibration, and the three metagene coordinates are tested without multiplicity discussion; (iv) the Sachs experiment is very small-scale and self-described as limited in scope.

The relation of the L^2-space partial covariance operator Sigma_{AB·C} = Sigma_AB - Sigma_AC Sigma_CB (vs. RKHS formulations with Sigma_CC^{-1}) to conditional independence is asserted via a footnote rather than a formal statement/proof, and the interplay between this characterization and the learned finite-dimensional features (which only capture a rank-d subspace) deserves more care — the test targets ||[[Sigma]]_d|| rather than the full operator, so d must be chosen large enough for signal capture, which is not verifiable in practice.

Presentation issues: several grammar/typo problems ('a algorithm', 'it in its training algorithm', 'Type 1 error' in Fig. 3), and notation is heavy (U both as matrix and operator, repeated redefinitions), which hampers readability of an already notation-dense paper.

strengths: The idea of extending spectral representation learning (Kostic et al., 2024) to partial covariance operators via a bi-level contrastive formulation is a sensible and reasonably novel way to address the scalability and adaptivity limits of kernel CI tests; the derivation of the bi-level variational formulation (Eqs. 5-8, Appendix A) is technically involved and clearly motivated by the fact that the Σ_XZ Σ_ZȲ term cannot be estimated directly.

The paper is upfront about the no-free-lunch obstacle (Shah & Peters, 2020) and frames its guarantees in terms of representation quality (E_val, E_pow) rather than overclaiming uniform validity; this is a more honest framing than many CI testing papers.

The experimental section is broad: post-nonlinear benchmarks against KCIT/RCIT/GCIT/DGCIT/NNLSCIT, a nonsmooth high-dimensional stress test, kernel-test comparisons, signal-strength ablations, a Sachs-inspired causal-discovery probe, runtime comparisons, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (Figs. 6-8).

The limitations section is candid about the lack of standard tuning protocols, conservative calibration in practice, and the fact that guarantees depend on learned-representation quality without explicit non-asymptotic rates.
weaknesses: The central operator-level claim is questionable: footnote 4 asserts that defining Σ_AB·C = Σ_AB − Σ_AC Σ_CB directly on L² spaces (without the normalization/inverses of Fukumizu et al. or Strobl et al.) still characterizes conditional independence (A ⊥⊥ B|C iff ‖Σ_A(B,C)·C‖_HS = 0). This equivalence holds for jointly Gaussian distributions but not in general: CI does not imply Cov(f(A), g(B)) factorizes through Σ_AC Σ_CB, and Σ_CC is not the identity on centered functions. Consequently the null hypothesis (9) tested by SpectralCIT is not equivalent to CI, and apparent validity must instead come from the adaptive feature learning nulling the residual (via the outer loss), which is not covered by the stated assumptions.

The main theorems appear internally inconsistent/incomplete. Theorem 4.1 claims validity assuming only E_val_m → 0, but the proof (Lemmas B.3-B.5, Appendix B.5-B.8) additionally requires d = o(√n), √d·E_m → 0, and n ≥ cK⁴d² log n; moreover E_val_m only measures orthonormality of learned features, not the approximation gap needed for Eq. (8) (i.e., that the learned features solve the bi-level problem well enough that the population residual vanishes under the null). Theorems 4.1/4.2 as stated do not follow from the hypotheses given.

The tuning protocol risks overfitting to the evaluation distributions: SpectralCIT's hyperparameters (including the test-time 'dimension pruning' fraction, drawn from Uniform(0.85,1)) are tuned with 30 Bayesian trials using the score S_val = type-I-error-minus-power on the same generative models later used for the headline comparisons. This makes the favorable calibration results in Figs. 2, 5, and 10 hard to interpret.

The TCGA-BRCA analysis has a likely train/test contamination issue: N = 1341 triplets are derived from only 135 WSIs (up to 10 patches per slide), yet the data are split 80/20 at the triplet level, so tiles from the same slide almost certainly appear in both the representation-learning and test sets, invalidating the p-value in Table 1. The strong rejection (p < 10⁻³) where KCIT and NNLSCIT do not reject could equally reflect miscalibration of the proposed test on this dataset rather than genuine residual signal.

Reproducibility is undermined: footnote 1 promises a code repository but the link is blank; given the many implementation degrees of freedom (whitening post-processing, pruning, bi-level alternation schedule), the missing code is a significant gap.

The empirical advantage over well-calibrated baselines is thin: the strongest competitor, NNLSCIT, matches SpectralCIT's type I error control and power on the main benchmark, and SpectralCIT is notably conservative in several settings (Figs. 3, 10, 11), sacrificing power; LPCIT was excluded for runtime reasons rather than compared.

Relative novelty is moderate: the outer loss, U-statistic estimation, whitening regularization, and analysis template closely follow Kostic et al. (2024) and Sun et al. (2025); the genuinely new element is the bi-level construction for the Σ_XZ Σ_ZȲ composition, and the statistical analysis largely re-verifies that the projected statistic behaves like a Gaussian quadratic form.

Presentation issues further weaken confidence: garbled statistic formula in Fig. 1, several typos ('a algorithm', 'in it its training algorithm', duplicated 'have have'), an apparent off-by-one in the spectral decomposition text of Appendix B.4, and dense operator derivations in the main text that obscure the key validity mechanism.

strengths: Well-motivated bridge between kernel-based CI testing and modern spectral/contrastive representation learning; the bi-level variational formulation for learning the truncated SVD of the partial covariance operator (Eqs. 5–8) is a genuinely nontrivial technical step, since the residualization term Σ_XZ Σ_ZŸ cannot be estimated directly from data.

The theoretical framing is sensible given the no-free-lunch result of Shah & Peters (2020): rather than imposing smoothness conditions, validity and power are characterized through the quality of learned representations (E_val and E_pow), with an asymptotic chi-squared null (Theorem 4.1) and a signal-strength condition for power (Theorem 4.2). The proof chain in Appendix B (spectral analysis of the projection, Lindeberg CLT, perturbation of eigenvalue bounds) is coherent and fairly careful.

Experiments are considerably more thorough than typical for CI testing papers: multiple synthetic benchmarks including a novel nonsmooth/oscillatory model that breaks NNLSCIT's assumptions, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, runtime comparison, a Sachs-inspired causal-discovery stress test, and a real TCGA breast cancer application. Honest limitations discussion covering calibration conservatism and the lack of non-asymptotic rates for learned representations.

The observed empirical behavior (competitors losing type I control in high dimensions while SpectralCIT stays calibrated but conservative) is consistent with the stated theory, and the signal-strength ablation directly supports Theorem 4.2.
weaknesses: Validity is conditional on a quantity that is neither verifiable nor bounded: type I error control requires E_val → 0, i.e., that the bi-level optimization actually learned near-orthonormal features with small approximation error, but no convergence or optimization-error bound is provided for Algorithm 1 (acknowledged in limitations). The guarantees are therefore more of a conditional characterization than a self-contained type I error guarantee.

The real-data experiment appears to violate the i.i.d. assumption underlying the entire analysis: the N = 1341 triplets come from only 135 WSIs/patients, with X (metagene scores) and Y (survival) constant within a patient and Z varying per tile. The triplets are strongly clustered, so the chi-squared null distribution does not apply and the p-value < 10^{-3} may be anti-conservative. No cluster-aware analysis or acknowledgment of this issue is given.

The L²-based partial covariance operator requires P_AB ≪ P_A × P_B (square-integrable Radon–Nikodym derivatives). This excludes natural deterministic or strongly dependent alternatives (e.g., X = f(Z), or X equal to a coordinate of Z), where the operator is ill-defined and the power guarantees are vacuous. The paper's claimed advantage over regression-based tests ('less restrictive') should be weighed against this structural restriction on the alternative class.
The code repository link in the manuscript is empty ('Code repository: .'), which undercuts reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter grids in Appendix C.

Presentation has noticeable defects: garbled statistic rendering in Figure 1, typos ('a algorithm', 'outputs' have', 'w.p.a.l.' used loosely, 'We have have'), inconsistent notation between E_pow defined as an operator norm error vs. its use in Theorem 4.2, and the proof-labeling glitches in Appendix B.4. Some claims, e.g., that sub-Gaussianity of learned features 'can be ensured by choosing bounded activations', gloss over the fact that training with unregularized objectives can still produce features whose covariance deviates from identity, which is exactly the quantity E_val that remains uncontrolled.

The diffusion-based baseline of Yang et al. (2025) is cited as the source of the benchmark model but does not appear in the reported comparisons; LPCIT is excluded only by footnote. Given that the benchmark is taken from Yang et al., a direct comparison would be expected.
